Part 1 of 6

Why the Economy Crashed

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Identify the major causes of the Great Depression.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, name two things that caused the Great Depression.

Reading ABuying on Margin and Black Tuesday

What made it so easy for so many to invest in stocks was the common practice of buying shares “on margin.” An investor could buy shares by making a small cash down payment (the “margin”) and borrow the rest from a stockbroker, who held the stock certificates as security in case the share price plummeted.

On what came to be called Black Tuesday, October 29—the worst day in stock market history—share prices went into free fall, and brokers found themselves flooded with stocks they could not sell. From October 23 to November 13, the market lost almost 40 percent of its value.

Word help: shares of stock = small pieces of a company · on margin = paying a little now and borrowing the rest · stockbroker = a person who buys and sells stocks for others · plummeted = fell fast · free fall = dropping with nothing to stop it

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Causes of the Great Depression” (The Roaring Stock Market of the 1920s; The Crash) (p. 1001).

Reading BToo Many Goods, Too Little Pay

The collapse of the stock market did not cause the Great Depression, however. Rather, it revealed that the prosperity of the 1920s had been built on unstable foundations.

The economy had actually begun to fall into a recession months before the stock market crash because of overproduction and underconsumption. During the 1920s, manufacturing production had increased by 43 percent, but the purchasing power of consumers had not kept pace. As a result, the economy was turning out more products than consumers could buy.

At the same time, many business owners had taken large profits while denying wage increases to employees. . . . Two-thirds of families in 1929 earned less than $2,000 annually. Inequality thus skyrocketed during the 1920s.

Word help: prosperity = good times with money · unstable foundations = a weak base · recession = a time when business slows down · overproduction = making too much · underconsumption = people buying too little · purchasing power = how much people can afford to buy

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Causes of the Great Depression” (Why the Economy Collapsed) (p. 1002).

Reading CGovernment Mistakes and a Weak Europe

The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 . . . sought to help the farm sector by raising tariffs on agricultural imports. . . . As predicted, the Smoot-Hawley Tariff prompted other countries to retaliate by passing tariffs of their own, thereby making it more difficult for American farms and businesses to sell their products abroad.

Instead of expanding the money supply to generate growth, the Federal Reserve tightened it out of concern for possible inflation in consumer prices. Between 1929 and 1932, the money supply shrank by a third, leading almost 10,000 small banks to close—and to take millions of depositors with them into bankruptcy.

Word help: tariff = a tax on goods from other countries · retaliate = strike back · Federal Reserve = the government agency that controls the money supply · money supply = the amount of money moving through the economy · depositors = people who keep money in a bank

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Causes of the Great Depression” (Government’s Action and the Economy; The European Influence) (p. 1003).

Part 2 of 6

Hard Times and Hoover’s Answer

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 2: Describe the impact of the Great Depression on the lives of the American people.

Core Objective 3: Explain how the Hoover administration failed to address the human distress caused by the Great Depression.

IN MY WORDS: How did the Depression hurt ordinary people, and what did President Hoover do (or not do) to help?

Reading DNo Jobs, No Food, No Home

As the economy spiraled downward, unemployment soared to record levels: 4 million in 1930, 8 million in 1931, and 12 million by 1932.

Surveys of children in the nation’s public schools in 1932 showed that one-quarter suffered from malnutrition. In a rural school in Appalachia, a teacher told a sickly child to go home and get something to eat. “I can’t,” she replied. “It’s my sister’s turn to eat.”

A thousand per day lost their homes to foreclosure, and millions were forced to move in with relatives or friends.

Word help: unemployment = not having a job · soared = went way up · malnutrition = sickness from not eating enough good food · foreclosure = a bank taking a home when the owner cannot pay

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Human Toll of the Depression” (Rising Unemployment; Hunger; Homelessness) (p. 1005).

Reading EHit Even Harder

As the Depression deepened, however, married women became the primary targets of layoffs. Twenty-six states passed laws prohibiting their employment, the reasoning being that a married woman should not “steal” a job from a husband and father.

In 1931, Hoover approved a plan to forcibly return Mexicans to Mexico. . . . Estimates vary widely, but at least 350,000 people—mostly factory laborers or farm workers and their families—were exiled to Mexico in the early 1930s. . . . An unknown number were American-born U.S. citizens who did not speak Spanish.

Word help: layoffs = losing a job because the boss cuts workers · prohibiting = not allowing · forcibly = by force · exiled = forced to leave the country · American-born = born in the United States

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Human Toll of the Depression” (Working Women; African Americans; Mexican Americans) (p. 1006).

Reading FThe Dust Bowl

In the southern plains of the Midwest and the Mississippi Valley, a terrible drought during the 1930s created a catastrophe known as the Dust Bowl. . . . As strong winds howled across treeless plains, they scooped up millions of tons of parched topsoil. Dark dust clouds floated eastward, engulfing farms and towns in what were called black blizzards.

Frequently lumped together as “Okies” or “Arkies,” most of the Dust Bowl refugees were from Cotton Belt communities in Arkansas, Texas, Missouri, and Oklahoma. During the 1930s and 1940s, some 800,000 people, mostly Whites, left those four states and headed to the Far West in search of jobs. . . . They discovered that rural California was no paradise. . . . As an Okie reported, when the big farmers “need us they call us migrants, and when we’ve picked their crop, we’re bums and we got to get out.”

Word help: drought = a long time with no rain · catastrophe = a terrible disaster · parched topsoil = dry top layer of farm dirt · engulfing = covering completely · migrants = people who move from place to place for work

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Human Toll of the Depression” (Dust Bowl Migrants) (p. 1008).

Picture 1Arriving in Bakersfield, 1935

Norton’s caption: “OKIES ON THE RUN A sharecropping family reaches its destination of Bakersfield, California, in 1935, after they ‘got blowed out in Oklahoma.’” (It is a primary source photo.)

What to look for: sharecropping family = farmers who worked someone else’s land for part of the crop · blowed out = forced out by the dust storms · look at = the people, the belongings tied to the car, and the car itself

Norton, Ch. 23, “The Human Toll of the Depression” (Dust Bowl Migrants), photo caption “Okies on the Run” (p. 1009). Primary source.

Picture 1. (1) What do you see tied to the outside of the car? (2) What does that tell you about this family’s move to California?

Reading GHoover Says No to Direct Help

By the fall of 1930, shantytowns sprouted in vacant lots where homeless people fashioned shacks out of cardboard and scrap wood and metal. There they shivered and suffered, calling their makeshift villages Hoovervilles in criticism of the president.

President Hoover refused any federal programs to help the needy directly for fear that the nation would be, as he said, “plunged into socialism.”

He pushed through Congress the Revenue Act of 1932, the largest—and most poorly timed—peacetime tax increase in history, raising the top rate from 24 percent to 63 percent. Taking money out of consumers’ pockets meant that they had less to spend when what the economy most needed was increased consumer spending.

Word help: shantytowns = towns of shacks · makeshift = quickly made from scraps · federal = run by the national government · socialism = government control of business and wealth · assistance = help

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “From Hooverism to the New Deal” (Short-Sighted Tax Increases; Hoover’s Response to the Social Crisis) (p. 1010).

Reading HHelp for Banks, Troops for Veterans

The new Congress that convened in 1931 demanded that President Hoover do more. He responded by proposing the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC), which Congress approved in 1932. The RFC made emergency loans to banks, life insurance companies, and railroads.

The Bonus Expeditionary Force, made up of members of the American Expeditionary Forces that had fought in France during the Great War, pressed Congress to pay the cash bonus owed to nearly 4 million veterans. . . . The soldiers, commanded by the army chief of staff, General Douglas MacArthur, removed the veterans from government buildings. . . . His soldiers rampaged through the unarmed veterans and their families, burning their flimsy shelters, terrorizing women, killing a baby, and bayoneting a boy chasing a rabbit.

Word help: emergency loans = money lent fast in a crisis · veterans = people who served in the military · bonus = extra money promised for service · rampaged = attacked wildly · bayoneting = stabbing with a blade on a rifle

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “From Hooverism to the New Deal” (Congressional Initiatives; Veterans in Protest) (p. 1012).

Part 3 of 6

The First New Deal

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Assess the goals and accomplishments of the First New Deal.

IN MY WORDS: What was Roosevelt trying to do in his first hundred days?

Reading IThe First Hundred Days

In March 1933, President Roosevelt confronted four major challenges: reviving the industrial economy, addressing the needs of record numbers of jobless and homeless Americans, rescuing the ravaged farm sector, and reforming the defects of the capitalist system that had contributed to the Depression.

From March 9, when the legislative session opened, to June 16, the so-called First Hundred Days, Congress approved fifteen major pieces of legislation proposed by Roosevelt. . . . Several of these programs constituted what came to be called the First New Deal (1933–1935).

Word help: confronted = faced · reviving = bringing back to life · ravaged = badly damaged · defects = flaws · legislation = laws

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “Roosevelt’s New Deal” (The First Hundred Days; Helping the Unemployed and Homeless) (p. 1016).

Reading JFixing Banks and Wall Street

On March 12, in the first of his many radio “fireside chats” to the nation, the president promised his 60 million listeners that it was safer to “keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress.” The following day, people took their money back to the banks.

On June 16, Roosevelt signed the Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933. It created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), through which the federal government insured customer bank accounts up to $2,500, thus reducing the likelihood of future panics.

The second bill, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, established the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to enforce the new laws and regulations governing the issuance and trading of stocks and bonds.

Word help: fireside chats = the president’s friendly radio talks · insured = promised to pay back if lost · panics = times when scared people pull out their money · regulations = rules · stocks and bonds = ways to invest money in companies

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “Roosevelt’s New Deal” (Banking Regulation; Regulating Wall Street) (p. 1017).

Reading KJobs, Factories, and Farms

The most successful New Deal jobs program was the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), managed by the War Department. . . . They planted 3 billion trees, taught farmers how to control soil erosion, and fought forest fires.

A second, more controversial part of the NIRA created the National Recovery Administration (NRA). . . . the NRA codes included “fair-labor” policies long sought by unions and social progressives: a national forty-hour workweek, minimum weekly wages of $13 ($12 in the South, where living costs were lower), and a ban on the employment of children under the age of sixteen.

The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 created the Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA), which sought to raise prices for crops and herds by paying farmers to cut production. . . . Farm income increased by 58 percent between 1932 and 1935.

Word help: conservation = protecting nature · soil erosion = dirt washing or blowing away · controversial = causing arguments · minimum wages = the lowest pay allowed · production = how much is grown or made

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “Roosevelt’s New Deal” (The CCC; Reviving the Industrial Sector; Agricultural Assistance) (p. 1019).

Source LWho Could Join the CCC? (Primary Source)

In 1936, the U.S. Department of Labor printed a handbook for the agents who chose young men for the Civilian Conservation Corps. This part tells who could join and why.

“An applicant for enrollment as a junior must be: Between 17 and 28 years of age, unmarried, unemployed, physically fit, a citizen of the United States, with needy dependents of blood or obligation, and willing to allot a substantial portion of the $30 minimum monthly cash allowance to a dependent beneficiary. . . . The group of young unmarried men is selected partly because of the type of work and the camp life involved, and partly because young unmarried men have had great difficulty in recent years in securing either work or relief. Some of them have never had the chance to have a job since they left school.”

Word help: applicant = a person who asks to join · enrollment = signing up · needy dependents = family members who need his help · allot = give a set part · allowance = pay · beneficiary = the person who gets the money · relief = help for the poor

U.S. Department of Labor, Handbook for Agencies Selecting Men for the Civilian Conservation Corps, 1936. In Norton, Ch. 23, “The New Deal Years: Hardships, Cultural Life, Criticism,” Comparing Perspectives: “Surviving the Great Depression” (p. 1029).

Source L. (1) Give two things a young man had to be to join the CCC. (2) Where did most of his $30 a month go?

Purpose. Why did the government want the CCC pay to go to the young man’s family instead of to him alone? Think about who else this helped.

Part 4 of 6

Culture and Critics

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Describe how the Depression was reflected in cultural life, and analyze the opposition to the First New Deal.

IN MY WORDS: How did books and movies show the Depression, and who attacked the New Deal?

Reading MFacing Hard Times or Escaping Them

For many writers and artists, the Depression inspired them to create art that dramatized the suffering experienced by so many, while plumbing the sources of social and economic inequality. By contrast, the more popular cultural forms (in particular, movies) provided entertainments—some funny and light-hearted, others nostalgic or filled with romance—that helped Americans escape the troubles of the day, if only for a short time.

To capture the ordeal of the Depression in The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Steinbeck traveled with some of the 3.5 million Okies who were fleeing the Dust Bowl to chase the false rumor that good jobs were to be had for the taking in the fields of California’s Central Valley.

Most feature films transported viewers into the escapist realms of adventure, spectacle, and fantasy. Gone with the Wind (1939), based on Margaret Mitchell’s Pulitzer Prize–winning novel, was a good example, as were The Wizard of Oz (1939) and Walt Disney’s Mickey Mouse cartoons.

Word help: dramatized = showed in a powerful way · inequality = some having much more than others · ordeal = a very hard experience · escapist = helping people forget their problems

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The New Deal Years: Hardships, Cultural Life, Criticism” (Cultural Life during the Depression; Literature; Movies) (p. 1030).

Reading NToo Much or Not Enough?

But Roosevelt was hated, too, especially by business leaders and political conservatives who believed the New Deal and the higher taxes it required were moving America toward socialism. Others, on the left, hated Roosevelt for not doing enough to end the Depression.

The most potent of the president’s populist opponents was Huey Pierce Long Jr., a colorful Democratic senator from Louisiana. . . . To launch his presidential candidacy, Long devised a simplistic plan called the Share-the-Wealth Society. He proposed to raise taxes on the wealthiest Americans and redistribute the revenue to “the people”—giving every poor family $5,000 and every wage worker an annual income of $2,500 . . . Another populist critic of President Roosevelt was Francis E. Townsend, a retired California doctor. . . . He wanted the federal government to pay $200 a month to every American over age sixty who agreed to quit working. . . . A third outspoken critic of FDR and the New Deal was Father Charles E. Coughlin . . . In fiery weekly broadcasts that attracted as many as 40 million listeners, he assailed the president as “anti-God” and claimed that the New Deal was a Communist conspiracy.

Word help: conservatives = people who want less government change · on the left = wanting more change and more help for the poor · redistribute = spread out again · revenue = money a government collects · assailed = attacked with words · conspiracy = a secret plan

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The New Deal Years: Hardships, Cultural Life, Criticism” (Critics Assault the New Deal; Huey Long; The Townsend Plan; Father Coughlin) (p. 1032).

Reading OUnfair Programs and a Hostile Court

For example, the payments from the AAA to farm owners to take land out of production in an effort to raise prices for farm products forced hundreds of thousands of tenant farmers and sharecroppers, both Black and White, off the land. . . . both the CCC and the TVA practiced racial segregation within their facilities.

By the end of its 1935–1936 term, the Supreme Court had ruled against New Deal programs in seven of nine major cases.

Word help: tenant farmers and sharecroppers = farmers who worked land owned by others · racial segregation = keeping races apart · ruled against = decided in court that something was not allowed

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The New Deal Years: Hardships, Cultural Life, Criticism” (African Americans and the New Deal; Opposition from the Supreme Court).

Part 5 of 6

The Second New Deal

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 6: Evaluate how the Second New Deal transformed the role of federal government in American life.

IN MY WORDS: Name one way the Second New Deal made the federal government bigger in people’s lives.

Reading PJobs and Unions

To rescue his legislative program from judicial and political challenges, in January 1935 President Roosevelt launched the Second New Deal, which was much more far-reaching than the First New Deal. He explained that “social justice . . . has become a definite goal.”

The first major initiative was the $4.8 billion Emergency Relief Appropriation Act. The largest peacetime spending bill in history to that point, it included an array of job programs to be managed by a new agency, the Works Progress Administration (WPA). . . . The WPA, headed by Harry Hopkins, quickly became the nation’s largest employer, hiring an average of 2 million people annually over four years.

Another major element of the Second New Deal was the National Labor Relations Act, often called the Wagner Act . . . Enacted in 1935, the legislation guaranteed workers the right to organize unions and bargain directly with management about wages and other issues.

Word help: far-reaching = affecting many people · social justice = fairness for all people · employer = a person or group that hires workers · bargain = talk to reach a deal · management = the bosses

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Second New Deal” (The WPA; The Wagner Act) (p. 1036).

Reading QSocial Security

The Great Depression hit the oldest Americans and those with disabilities especially hard. To address these problems, FDR proposed the Social Security Act of 1935. Social Security, he announced, was the “cornerstone” of the New Deal, its “supreme achievement.”

The act’s centerpiece was a federal retirement fund for people over age sixty-five. Beginning in 1937, workers and employers contributed monthly payroll taxes to establish the fund.

In addition, the Social Security system excluded 9.5 million low-paid workers who most needed it: farm laborers, domestic workers (maids and cooks), and the self-employed, a disproportionate percentage of whom were African Americans.

Word help: cornerstone = the most important part · retirement fund = money saved for people who stop working when old · payroll taxes = taxes taken out of paychecks · excluded = left out · domestic workers = people who work in others’ homes

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Second New Deal” (Social Security; Provisions of the Social Security Act; Limitations and Critics) (p. 1037).

Picture 2A Social Security Poster

Norton’s caption: “SOCIAL SECURITY The federal government distributed posters such as this one to educate the public about the new Social Security Act.” The small print says who is eligible: “everybody working for salary or wages (with only a few exceptions, such as agriculture, domestic service, and government work).” (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: eligible = allowed to get it · salary or wages = pay for work · exceptions = people left out · agriculture = farm work · domestic service = work as maids and cooks

Norton, Ch. 23, “The Second New Deal” (Provisions of the Social Security Act), poster with caption “Social Security” (p. 1038). Primary source.

Picture 2. (1) What does the poster promise, and starting at what age? (2) Which workers does the poster say are left out? Who would that hurt most, according to Reading Q?

Reading RA Halfway Revolution

During the 1930s, for the first time in peacetime, the federal government assumed responsibility for planning and managing the economy and intervening to ensure social stability. By the end of the 1930s, the power and scope of the national government had vastly increased over what they had been in 1932. . . . Most important, however, the New Deal restored a sense of hope to many people who had grown discouraged and desperate.

The greatest failure of the New Deal was its inability to restore prosperity and end record levels of unemployment. In 1939, some 10 million Americans—nearly 17 percent of the workforce—remained jobless. Only the prolonged crisis of World War II and its attendant military and industrial needs would at last bring full employment to the United States.

Word help: assumed responsibility = took on the job · intervening = stepping in · scope = how far something reaches · restored = brought back · prolonged = long-lasting · full employment = almost everyone who wants a job has one

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 23, “The Second New Deal” (A Halfway Revolution) (p. 1044).
